notes: One-line meanings of plant-info words on the crop page and Bees tracker. Each term links to a lesson. Bee words were added in v2. v3 writes out short forms in term titles (for example nucleus colony (nuc), honey box (super), package of bees, varroa mites). Published remotely at GT_CONFIG.GLOSSARY_DATA_URL.

terms.definition: A plant that lives for more than two years and can grow back each year.
A plant that grows, makes seed, and dies in one growing season.
A plant that grows leaves in year one and flowers and seeds in year two.
A crop that grows best in warm weather and is hurt by frost.
A crop that grows best in cool weather and can take a light frost.
A group of related plants that often share the same bugs and diseases.
Planting seeds in the soil where the plants will grow.
A young plant started in a pot, then moved to the garden.
A piece of root with buds, used to start plants like asparagus.
A tree or shrub sold with no soil on its roots.
A tree sold in a pot with soil already around its roots.
These are potato pieces with eyes. You plant them to grow new plants.
About how many days until you can pick the crop.
How far apart to set plants so each one has room to grow.
At least six hours of direct sun each day.
About three to six hours of direct sun each day.
How many hours of direct sun a plant gets each day.
This tells how cold winters get. It helps you pick plants that can live there.
The smallest pot volume a plant needs so its roots have room.
Moving pollen to a flower so fruit or seed can form.
A plant that can set fruit with pollen from its own variety.
A plant needs pollen from a second kind to make fruit.
A scale that tells how hot a pepper tastes. Higher numbers mean more heat.
This is how many years you wait. Then the tree or bush makes fruit.
A frame, stake, or cage that holds a plant up off the ground.
The young bees still in the comb: eggs, larvae, and pupae.
Brood cells that bees have sealed with wax while the young bee finishes growing.
A large, peanut-shaped cell where a new queen is being raised.
A queen cell built when the colony is getting ready to swarm, or split and fly off.
A box stacked on the hive where bees store extra honey you may harvest. Beekeepers often call this a “super.”
The main hive box where the queen lays eggs and the bees raise brood (the young bees).
A small starter hive, often with a queen, workers, and a few frames of comb already built. People often say “nuc” for short.
A screened box of worker bees, with a queen in a cage, sold to start a hive. People often say “package” for short.
A removable wooden or plastic rectangle that holds the comb in the hive.
A thin sheet of wax or plastic in a frame that guides bees as they build comb.
Tiny mites that feed on honey bees and their brood and can weaken a hive.
A test that washes mites off a sample of bees so you can count them. An alcohol or soap wash is the more reliable kind. People also use a powdered-sugar roll.
A male honey bee. Drones do not sting and do not gather food.
A female honey bee that does the work of the hive, including foraging and raising brood.
A sticky mix of plant resins that bees use to seal cracks in the hive.
A small can that makes cool smoke to calm bees while you inspect the hive.
A block that makes the hive door smaller, so bees can guard it more easily.
A metal or sturdy strip at the entrance that keeps mice out in the cold season.
A serious brood disease, including American foulbrood and European foulbrood. In many places you must report it to a bee inspector.
A pest or disease you must report to the local bee inspector or farm office if you find it, or even if you only suspect it.
